description: First eval sets for saudi-arabia-grc and uae-grc (August 2026). Assertions authored from the Phase-0 primary-source facts sheets (NCA ECC-2:2024, SDAIA PDPL + regulations, CST framework, SAMA CSF; UAE PDPL status, DIFC Amendment Law 1/2025, ADGM DPR, CBUAE circulars, ICT Health Law). Post-cutoff ground truths embedded for graders. Prompts exercise the ROUTER (jurisdiction/sector applicability), not framework recall.

evals.prompt: We are a European e-commerce retailer opening a Saudi entity and an online store for Saudi customers. No government contracts. What Saudi regulations apply to us, and what should our first 90 days of compliance work look like?
assertions: Delivers an applicability determination BEFORE detail: Saudi PDPL applies (personal data of Saudi residents); NCA ECC-2:2024 is NOT mandatory for a private non-CNI retailer (recommended best practice only); SAMA and CST licensing regimes do not apply to a plain retailer — each conclusion tied to the right regulator (SDAIA / NCA / SAMA / CST)
States the PDPL enforcement reality: Royal Decree M/19 as amended by M/148, fully enforced since September 14, 2024, with SDAIA actively enforcing (first-wave violation decisions issued in 2025-26)

Names concrete PDPL first-90-days actions: controller registration on SDAIA's National Data Governance Platform, RoPA, lawful bases (including the M/148 legitimate-interest basis for non-sensitive data), privacy notices, and a transfer mechanism for EU-KSA data flows (SDAIA SCC modules / adequacy / BCRs)
States the breach-notification rule correctly: 72 hours to SDAIA (via the platform), with data-subject notification where they are at risk

States penalty exposure correctly: fines up to SAR 5M per violation (doubling for repeat), with criminal exposure for unlawful disclosure of sensitive data — without inventing enacted amendments (the 2025 graduated-penalty proposals are not enacted as of August 2026; a compliant answer either omits them or flags them as pending)

evals.prompt: We are a fintech licensed by SAMA. Do the NCA Essential Cybersecurity Controls also apply to us, or only the SAMA framework? What maturity level do we need?
assertions: Answers the stacking question correctly: SAMA CSF applies to all SAMA-regulated entities (including licensed fintechs); NCA ECC additionally applies only if the entity owns/operates/hosts Critical National Infrastructure — the regimes stack rather than displace, and the answer must not claim ECC is mandatory for every fintech
States the SAMA CSF structure accurately: 4 domains (Leadership & Governance; Risk Management & Compliance; Operations & Technology; Third-Party Cyber Security)
States the maturity expectation correctly: 6-level maturity model (0-5) with SAMA expecting minimum maturity level 3
Notes that PDPL applies in parallel for customer personal data (SDAIA, distinct from SAMA)

Gives practical unify-and-map advice: maintain one internal control set mapped to both SAMA CSF and ECC (if CNI) rather than duplicate programmes, and confirm CNI designation status rather than assuming

evals.prompt: We are a global SaaS provider planning to host workloads for a Saudi government ministry on our cloud. What must we comply with, and where must the data live?
assertions: Identifies the full stack for a CSP serving government: CST Cloud Computing Regulatory Framework registration (class determines permissible data levels), NCA CCC provider-side controls (as the ministry is ECC-covered), and PDPL for any personal data — all three named with their regulators

States the residency rule decisively: government data must remain in-Kingdom (localization is exclusive, narrow exceptions) — an answer suggesting offshore hosting of ministry workloads with contractual fixes FAILS this assertion
Explains the classification-driven model: cloud levels tied to data classification (Top Secret/Secret/Confidential/Public) and CST customer-data Levels with Levels 3-4 requiring in-Kingdom hosting
Reflects the CCC's role-split design: provider-side vs tenant-side controls (e.g., P vs T control markers), with the ministry remaining accountable as tenant — no invented control IDs

Gives a realistic sequencing: CST registration/class, in-Kingdom infrastructure or partnership, CCC control implementation with evidence, then contract with the ministry — including Arabic-language/local-presence practicalities where relevant

evals.prompt: A marketing employee at our Riyadh company emailed a spreadsheet of 40,000 customer records including national IDs to an external vendor without authorization. Walk us through our obligations under Saudi law.
assertions: States the core clock correctly: notify SDAIA within 72 hours of becoming aware, via the National Data Governance Platform, and notify affected data subjects where the breach risks harm to them

Frames the incident correctly as a PDPL personal-data breach / unauthorized disclosure (national IDs + customer records), engaging containment (recall/delete demands to the vendor, access revocation) and evidence preservation before/alongside notification

Covers the vendor dimension: whether the vendor is an authorized processor under a compliant processing arrangement matters; unauthorized disclosure to a third party is itself a violation category SDAIA has enforced against

States realistic consequences: administrative fines up to SAR 5M (doubling on repeat), SDAIA's active enforcement posture (first-wave decisions 2025-26), and criminal exposure reserved for sensitive-data disclosure (and correctly does NOT claim national IDs alone are 'sensitive data' under the PDPL's sensitive categories)
Includes accountability follow-through: document the incident, root-cause and remediate (DLP/training/access), update RoPA and vendor contracts

evals.prompt: We already hold ISO 27001:2022. How much of NCA ECC-2:2024 does that cover, and what specifically remains for a Saudi government subsidiary?
assertions: States ECC applicability correctly for this entity: as a government subsidiary, ECC-2:2024 is MANDATORY (not merely recommended)

Describes ECC-2:2024's structure accurately: 4 domains (Governance; Defense; Resilience; Third-Party & Cloud), 28 subdomains, 108 main controls (+92 subcontrols), control IDs in domain-subdomain-control format — and does not invent specific control IDs

Gives a credible ISO mapping: ISO 27001:2022 Annex A covers much of Governance/Defense/Third-Party thematically, and certification evidence can be reused — but ISO certification does NOT constitute ECC compliance

Names Saudi-specific deltas ISO does not satisfy: NCA compliance-tool reporting/self-assessment mechanics and NCA audits, Arabic-language governance artifacts where required, KSA residency/cloud rules for government data (CCC/CST), and OT/telework/data siblings (OTCC/TCC/DCC) where in scope
Recommends the right process: map Annex A controls to ECC domains, gap-assess the uncovered ECC controls, and prepare NCA-facing evidence — structured as a gap table with evidence columns

evals.prompt: We are a fintech licensed in the DIFC. Which data protection law applies to us — the UAE federal PDPL or something else? What changed in 2025 that we should worry about?
assertions: Routes correctly: DIFC entities are excluded from the federal PDPL — the DIFC Data Protection Law No. 5 of 2020 applies, overseen by the DIFC Commissioner of Data Protection
States the 2025 change accurately: Amendment Law No. 1 of 2025, in force July 15, 2025 — the biggest update since 2020

Names the amendment's key risk shift: a statutory PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION for data subjects (GDPR-style claims exposure), plus documented transfer-adequacy assessments and Commissioner power to review/withdraw adequacy decisions

Mentions the raised fine tiers accurately (e.g., new USD 25,000-50,000 tiers for failure to notify processing or conduct required DPIAs) and ongoing duties: annual notification/registration with the Commissioner, DPO for high-risk processing, breach notification
Keeps regulators straight: prudential/conduct supervision for a DIFC fintech sits with the DFSA — the answer must not cite CBUAE rules unless the firm is separately CBUAE-licensed

evals.prompt: We are a US healthtech SaaS selling to a private hospital in Dubai. Can the hospital's patient data live in our US-hosted cloud? What UAE rules govern this?
assertions: Leads with the decisive rule: the ICT Health Law (Federal Law 2/2019) generally PROHIBITS storing/processing/transferring UAE health data outside the UAE — default answer: patient data cannot live in a US-hosted cloud

States the exception pathway correctly: exceptions require authorization via the relevant health authority and MOHAP (Cabinet Decision 32/2020; Ministerial Resolution 51/2021 covers approved cases such as specified telemedicine) — not fixable by contracts alone
Quantifies exposure: localization violations carry fines of AED 500,000-700,000
Routes to the right authority for a Dubai private hospital (DHA, with MOHAP at federal level) and notes the law prevails over the federal PDPL via the health-data carve-out

Gives the practical architecture answer: in-UAE hosting (or an authorized exception) for patient data, with a split analysis for non-health personal data (federal PDPL readiness posture) — and advises the vendor to verify current authority guidance before promising any exception

evals.prompt: Our mainland Dubai retail company wants to get ahead of UAE privacy law. What is actually enforceable today, and what should we build now?
assertions: States the pivotal status fact accurately and with a date: the federal PDPL (Decree-Law 45/2021) has been in force since January 2, 2022, but its EXECUTIVE REGULATIONS remain unissued as of August 2026 — penalties and operational detail await them, and enforcement is effectively dormant. FAIL any answer asserting the regulations are issued or citing enacted PDPL fine amounts
States the grace mechanism: organizations get a 6-month compliance period from the regulations' issuance — which is exactly why readiness work should start now

Correctly scopes what DOES bite a mainland retailer today: the cybercrime law (Federal Decree-Law 34/2021), sector rules if applicable, and contractual/counterparty expectations — not zone DP laws (DIFC/ADGM excluded and irrelevant to a mainland retailer)

Prescribes a sensible GDPR-family readiness build: data inventory/RoPA, lawful-basis and consent design, privacy notices, DPO assessment, breach-response playbook, transfer mapping — framed as preparation for the regulations
Notes the carve-outs correctly (government data, health data under the ICT Health Law, banking/credit data under CBUAE rules, DIFC/ADGM) when describing the PDPL's scope

evals.prompt: We are an ADGM-based asset manager. A laptop with client personal data was stolen. What are our notification obligations and deadlines?
assertions: Applies the right law: ADGM Data Protection Regulations 2021 (not the federal PDPL, not DIFC law), overseen by the ADGM Office of Data Protection / Commissioner
States the deadline correctly: notify the Commissioner within 72 HOURS of becoming aware of the breach, and notify affected data subjects where there is high risk to them

Covers incident mechanics: assess scope (encryption status of the laptop matters to risk), contain (remote wipe, credential rotation), preserve evidence, and document the incident and decision-making even if notification is judged unnecessary
Notes the parallel regulator: as an FSRA-regulated asset manager, operational-incident expectations to FSRA run alongside the DP notification — and the answer must not cite CBUAE
Includes follow-through: root-cause remediation (encryption, MDM), RoPA/security-policy updates, and annual-notification standing with the ODP

evals.prompt: Our CBUAE-licensed bank wants to move its core banking system and customer data to a cloud provider whose regional data centers are in Bahrain. What approvals and constraints apply?
assertions: Leads with the residency constraint: under the CBUAE Consumer Protection Regulation (Circular 8/2020) and Standards, consumer/transaction data must be stored and processed WITHIN the UAE — Bahrain-hosted consumer data conflicts with this baseline
States the transfer gate correctly: sharing/transferring confidential consumer data outside the UAE requires CBUAE approval AND prior written customer consent — not merely contractual safeguards

Applies the Outsourcing Regulation (Circular 14/2021): material outsourcing (core banking to cloud qualifies) needs CBUAE approval before implementation, with a Master System of Record maintained in the UAE, retained data ownership, and mandatory audit/on-site inspection rights (bank and CBUAE) plus breach-notification and exit clauses

Gives the realistic architecture conclusion: in-UAE hosting (e.g., UAE regions/data centers) for consumer data with any offshore elements limited to non-consumer data or explicitly approved arrangements — an answer waving Bahrain hosting through FAILS
Adds the parallel tracks: federal PDPL readiness posture (banking-data carve-out notwithstanding) and operational-resilience/security expectations, with early CBUAE engagement advised on timeline
